The paper proposes IM-ENGINE, a pipeline that uses image editing applied to simulator-rendered scenes as a bridge between semantic intent and physical robot execution. By keeping an anchor object unchanged, it recovers metric 3D state from the edited image, refines it with physics simulation, and converts it into robot grasps or goal placements.

IM-ENGINE bridges the gap between semantic intent and physical execution in robot learning by using generative image editing inside a simulator loop. By editing simulator-rendered scenes and grounding those edits back into 3D physics, the pipeline automatically scales the generation of high-quality training data for complex tasks like functional dexterous grasping and precise object placement.

## What Problem Does This Paper Address?

To teach robots how to manipulate objects in the real world, we need training data that is both semantically meaningful (e.g., holding a spray bottle by the handle with a finger on the trigger) and physically executable (e.g., not dropping the bottle).

We present a pipeline for grasp selection and force regulation in a five-fingered robotic hand, based on a map of locally admissible contact loads. From an operator command, the system identifies the target object, reconstructs its 3D geometry using SAM3D, and imports the model into Isaac Sim. jina.title: IM-ENGINE: Image Editing for Embodied Data Generation
jina.snippet:
[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.06279)[HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.06279v1)

> Abstract:Learning-based manipulation requires supervision that is both semantically meaningful and physically executable, but current data pipelines often provide only one of these properties. Human demonstrations capture intent but are costly to collect and constrained by the human-robot embodiment gap, while simulation can scale data generation but often under-specifies functional behavior. We present IM-ENGINE, a simulator-grounded pipeline that uses image editing as an intermediate representation for embodied data generation. Given a rendered scene with known geometry, depth, segmentation, and camera parameters, IM-ENGINE edits the image to inject task-relevant semantics, recovers explicit 3D state using simulator priors and an unchanged anchor object, refines the state in physics, and converts it into robot-executable supervision. We instantiate the pipeline for dexterous grasp synthesis and goal-state generation. For grasping, IM-ENGINE generates a human grasp in image space, recovers the hand-object interaction, retargets it to a robot hand, and refines it into physically validated robot grasps. For goal generation, it edits a rendered scene into a desired outcome, recovers the target-object pose, and refines it into physically valid, semantically meaningful goals and trajectories. This combination of generative semantic priors and simulator grounding enables scalable task-relevant supervision for robot learning.

octen.snippet:
Computer Science > Robotics

arXiv:2609.31207 (cs)

[Submitted on 25 Sep 2026]
Title: Enabling a Unified Cross-Domain Representation for Two-Finger Gripper Manipulation via Interaction-Centric Modeling

Authors: Guanlin Li, Shifeng Bao, Yihan Zhao, Haitao Shen, Haoyang Li, Chen Zhao, Tong Yang, Jie Tang, Jing Zhang

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Achieving robust cross-embodiment generalization in imitation learning demands overcoming a critical representation flaw that inextricably entangles task semantics with hardware-specific visual geometry. We propose an interaction-centric framework that leverages the shared structure of two-finger grippers via a parameterized universal gripper abstraction, yielding a canonical gripper-frame representation. Given language and RGB-D observations, a VLM infers the subtask and grounds an interaction triplet (gripper, held, target), while SAM~2.1 tracks masks to reduce VLM queries. We design concise hybrid features that combine target/collision artificial potential fields for global guidance with segmented gripper-frame point clouds for local geometry, and use a Flow-Matching Transformer to predict smooth 7-DoF action chunks. Experiments in simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that ours is the first imitation learning approach to simultaneously achieve competitive benchmark scores and extreme cross-embodiment/cross-viewpoint zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to completely distinct, heterogeneous robot platforms.

octen.snippet:
ROBOWHEEL: A HELICAL DATA ENGINE FROM REAL-WORLD HUMAN DEMONSTRATIONS FOR CROSS-DOMAIN ROBOTIC LEARNING
Keywords: robot Learning, human and object reconstruction
Abstract: We introduce robowheel, a helical data engine that converts in-the-wild human hand–object interaction (HOI) videos into training-ready supervision for cross-morphology robotic learning. From monocular RGB/RGB-D inputs, we perform high-precision HOI reconstruction and enforce physical plausibility via a reinforcement learning optimizer that refines hand–object relative poses under contact and penetration constraints. The reconstructed, contact-rich trajectories are then retargetted to cross-domain embodiments, robot arms with simple end-effectors, dexterous hands, and humanoids, yielding executable actions and rollouts. To scale coverage, we build a simulation-augmented framework on Isaac Sim with diverse domain randomization (body variants, trajectories, object replacement, background changes, hand motion mirroring), which expands observations and labels while preserving contact semantics. This process forms an end-to-end pipeline from video → reconstruction → retargeting → augmentation → data acquisition, closing the loop for iterative policy improvement. Across vision-language-action and imitation-learning settings, \nbname-generated data provides reliable supervision and consistently improves task performance over baselines, enabling direct use of Internet HOI videos (hand-only or upper-body) as labels for scenario-specific training. We further assemble a large-scale multimodal dataset combining multi-camera captures, monocular videos, and public HOI corpora, and demonstrate transfer on dexterous-hand and humanoid platforms.

* 人类演示数据天然携带功能语义（如抓喷壶要按扳机、挂杯子要挂到杯架上），但采集成本高、受限于人机具身差异，难以直接迁移到机器人。

* 本文目标是将图像编辑作为语义接口嵌入仿真闭环，使生成内容既能表达任务意图，又能通过仿真先验恢复度量 3D 状态并经过物理验证，最终输出机器人可用的抓取、目标位姿和轨迹。

###### Abstract

Learning-based manipulation requires supervision that is both semantically meaningful and physically executable, but current data pipelines often provide only one of these properties. Human demonstrations capture intent but are costly to collect and constrained by the human–robot embodiment gap, while simulation can scale data generation but often under-specifies functional behavior. We present IM-ENGINE, a simulator-grounded pipeline that uses image editing as an intermediate representation for embodied data generation. Given a rendered scene with known geometry, depth, segmentation, and camera parameters, IM-ENGINE edits the image to inject task-relevant semantics, recovers explicit 3D state using simulator priors and an unchanged anchor object, refines the state in physics, and converts it into robot-executable supervision. We instantiate the pipeline for dexterous grasp synthesis and goal-state generation. For grasping, IM-ENGINE generates a human grasp in image space, recovers the hand-object interaction, retargets it to a robot hand, and refines it into physically validated robot grasps. For goal generation, it edits a rendered scene into a desired outcome, recovers the target-object pose, and refines it into physically valid, semantically meaningful goals and trajectories. This combination of generative semantic priors and simulator grounding enables scalable task-relevant supervision for robot learning.

We first introduce a scalable annotation pipeline that automatically enriches hand-object interaction datasets with fine-grained structured language labels capturing interaction intent. Building upon these annotations, AffordGrasp integrates an affordance-aware latent representation of hand poses with a dual-conditioning diffusion process, enabling the model to jointly reason over object geometry, spatial affordances, and instruction semantics. A distribution adjustment module further enforces physical contact consistency and semantic alignment. seltz.snippet:
**Short answer:** A vision-language-action (VLA) model turns camera observations and a natural-language goal into robot actions through a learned policy. Traditional robot programming spells out the task, motion, sensing conditions, and safety responses in explicit software such as state machines, behavior trees, PLC logic, planners, and feedback controllers. VLAs can make robots more adaptable to new wording, objects, and arrangements, but their behavior is probabilistic and must be bounded by conventional safety and control systems. For a fixed, repetitive, safety-critical cell, explicit programming is usually easier to verify. For changing scenes and many task variations, a VLA—or a hybrid stack that combines one with classical control—is often more practical.

## What a vision-language-action model is

A VLA is a robot policy whose core inputs include visual observations and a natural-language instruction, and whose output is an action representation for the robot. A camera image might show a workbench, while an instruction says, “Pick up the blue cup and place it beside the plate.” The model interprets both together and produces actions such as end-effector movements, gripper commands, joint targets, or tokens that a downstream action decoder converts into control values.

Implementations differ. Some emit discrete action tokens autoregressively; others produce continuous controls, diffusion samples, flow-matched actions, or a high-level action that another policy executes. A VLA may also consume proprioception—joint positions, velocities, force readings, or gripper state—and additional sensors. What makes it a VLA is that visual information and language are central to the policy’s action generation, rather than language merely selecting a prewritten routine.

Learning-based manipulation requires supervision that is both semantically meaningful and physically executable, but current data pipelines often provide only one of these properties. Human demonstrations capture intent but are costly to collect and constrained by the human–robot embodiment gap, while simulation can scale data generation but often under-specifies functional behavior. This combination of generative semantic priors and simulator grounding enables scalable task-relevant supervision for robot learning.

The objective of this research is to bridge this gap by developing **IM-ENGINE**, a pipeline that leverages generative image editing as an intermediate representation to produce scalable, high-fidelity **embodied data generation** for robotic manipulation tasks.
**2. METHODOLOGY / APPROACH**
The researchers propose a **simulator-grounded pipeline** that utilizes rendered scenes containing known **geometry, depth maps, semantic segmentation, and camera intrinsic/extrinsic parameters**. The IM-ENGINE framework operates through a multi-stage process: first, it applies generative image editing to inject task-relevant semantics into a rendered scene; second, it recovers the explicit **3D state** of objects and agents using **simulator priors** and anchor object tracking; third, it performs **physics-based refinement** to ensure contact stability and kinematic feasibility; and finally, it converts these refined states into robot-executable supervision. The methodology was instantiated through two primary use cases: **dexterous grasp synthesis** (retargeting human hand-object interactions to robot end-effectors) and **goal-state generation** (editing scenes to represent desired outcomes).
**3. FINDINGS / RESULTS**
IM-ENGINE successfully demonstrates that image-space semantic manipulation can be transformed into valid physical trajectories. In **grasp synthesis**, the pipeline effectively captures human grasp intent from 2D edits, recovers the complex **hand-object interaction**, and retargets these poses to a robot hand while ensuring physical validity through simulation refinement. For **goal generation**, the system successfully translates visual "desired outcomes" into precise target-object poses and semantically meaningful trajectories that respect the laws of physics. This confirms that generative semantic priors can be effectively grounded in rigid-body dynamics.

webiq.snippet:
We present IM-ENGINE, a simulator-grounded pipeline that uses image editing as an intermediate representation for embodied data generation. Given a rendered scene with known geometry, depth, segmentation, and camera parameters, IM-ENGINE edits the image to inject task-relevant semantics, recovers explicit 3D state using simulator priors and an unchanged anchor object, refines the state in physics, and converts it into robot-executable supervision. We instantiate the pipeline for dexterous grasp synthesis and goal-state generation. For grasping, IM-ENGINE generates a human grasp in image space, recovers the hand-object interaction, retargets it to a robot hand, and refines it into physically validated robot grasps. For goal generation, it edits a rendered scene into a desired outcome, recovers the target-object pose, and refines it into physically valid, semantically meaningful goals and trajectories. 

Edited images are grounded back into simulator state for two tasks: functional dexterous grasp synthesis and goal-state generation, yielding physically validated grasps, goals, and robot-usable trajectories.

- Figure 2: Our pipeline consists of four stages: (a) image generation edits a simulator-rendered scene according to the task, producing a visual proposal for either a functional grasp or a target goal arrangement; (b) perception lifts the edited image into a structured 3D state using simulator priors and anchor-based metric depth alignment; (c) physics validation filters and refines the state for contact, stability, and collision feasibility; and (d) trajectory generation converts validated states into robot manipulation data for dexterous grasp synthesis and goal-state reaching.
